2. The pain occurs 1–2 times per week, lasts for several hours, and is unrelated to specific activities, but it affects her ability to concentrate at work and fall asleep.
3. She denies nipple discharge.
4. Her menstrual cycles are regular, occurring every 28 days with normal flow, and her last period was one week ago.
5. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms consistently.
6. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications.
7. She consumes 2–4 glasses of wine on weekends and does not smoke or use illicit drugs.
8. Her maternal grandmother had aortic valve stenosis in her 70s, but there is no other relevant family history.
9. Physical examination reveals a BMI of 24 kg/m², normal vital signs, and no visible skin or nipple abnormalities.
10. There is mild tenderness in the lower outer quadrant of the left breast, but no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy.
11. The rest of the examination, including cardiopulmonary findings, is unremarkable.
12. ECG shows regular sinus rhythm with no acute abnormalities.

D. Evening primrose oil supplementation  
E. MRI of the breast  
F. Diagnostic core needle biopsy  
G. Watchful waiting for 3 months  
H. Hormonal contraceptive therapy  
I. Referral to breast surgeon  
J. Oral contraceptive therapy

3. Laser peripheral iridotomy had been performed but failed to deepen the AC.  
4. Subsequently, a choroidal mass was discovered, and he was referred for our opinion.  
5. On examination, refractive error was +3.00 D OU, and best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/40 OS.  
6. Results of examination in the right eye were unremarkable, and IOP was 17 mm Hg.  
7. Examination of the left eye revealed elevated IOP of 26 mm Hg while the patient was taking dorzolamide/timolol.  
8. The AC was shallow, and episcleral vessels were congested.  
9. Ophthalmoscopic examination and wide-angle scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (Figure 1A) documented a ring-shaped peripheral ciliochoroidal mass accompanied by shallow serous retinal detachment inferiorly.  
10. Globe transillumination revealed an undefined mottled choroidal shadow inferiorly.  
11. B-scan ultrasonography (Figure 1B) and ultrasound biomicroscopy suggested an echolucent ciliochoroidal elevation without intrinsic vascular pulsations.  
12. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits confirmed the ring-shaped ciliochoroidal elevation with nonenhancement of the mass.  
13. Doppler ultrasonography showed normal flow parameters without evidence of a dural-cavernous fistula.  
14. A, Wide-angle fundus photograph demonstrating peripheral choroidal elevation, most prominent superotemporally, and numerous choroidal folds.

16. Proceed with sclerotomies, ie, creation of scleral windows

1. An African American woman in her 50s presented for recent-onset blurred vision in both eyes for 2 months.
2. She endorsed mild photophobia but denied pain, redness, tearing, or discharge.
3. There was no history of oral/genital ulcers, rashes, or atopy.
4. Her medical history was significant for hypertension, asthma, hepatitis C, and essential tremor.
5. Her medications include lisinopril, albuterol sulfate, and amantadine hydrochloride.
6. She denied any previous ocular surgical procedures or trauma.
7. She was seen 2 weeks prior and was treated with 400 mg of oral acyclovir sodium 5 times a day and sodium chloride, 5%, ointment 4 times a day.
8. Her central corneal thickness at that time was recorded at 798 μm OD and 827 μm OS.
9. Her best-corrected visual acuity at presentation was 20/70 OD and 20/50 OS.
10. Her extraocular motility, pupils, and confrontation visual fields were normal.
11. Intraocular pressures were 7 and 9 mm Hg OD and OS, respectively.
12. An anterior segment slitlamp examination was significant for central bilateral stromal edema, Descemet folds, microcystic edema, and endothelial guttae in both eyes (Figure).
13. There were no keratic precipitates, and the anterior chamber did not show cells or flare.
14. Conjunctiva was white and quiet.
15. No abnormalities were noted during an ophthalmoscopic examination.
16. Her central corneal thickness was found to be 833 μm OD and 925 μm OS.
17. Slitlamp photograph at presentation showing corneal edema in the left eye.
18. Corneal edema was similar in both eyes.

1. A woman in her late 50s was referred to the neuro-ophthalmology clinic for evaluation of a 7-month history of recurrent, transient vision loss in the right eye.
2. She reported 5 episodes, each lasting a few minutes and all occurring on awakening.
3. Further inquiry revealed that symptoms always developed after using her electronic reader tablet in dim lighting while lying on her left side.
4. Notably, the patient reported immediate resolution of vision loss on turning on the lights.
5. She denied headaches, visual aura, or neurologic symptoms.
6. Her other medical history was unremarkable.
7. Six months prior to presentation, workup at her local hospital for the transient vision loss revealed an enhancing right orbital mass on magnetic resonance imaging (Figure, A).
8. Carotid ultrasonography and head magnetic resonance angiography showed no abnormalities.
9. Inflammatory marker levels were normal.
10. Magnetic resonance imaging 3 months later showed a stable mass without change in size or appearance.
11. A, T1-weighted magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the orbit with contrast shows a well-circumscribed, enhancing soft-tissue lesion in the right orbit superomedially (arrowhead).
12. B, Computed tomographic (CT) scan of the orbit with contrast shows the mass (arrowhead); no change noted on Valsalva maneuver.
13. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 OD.
14. Pupils, intraocular pressure, and motility were unremarkable.
15. Anterior segment examination showed mild cataract and dry eye.
16. Posterior pole examination revealed evidence of posterior vitreous detachment and normal optic nerves with 0.2 cup-to-disc ratio in each eye.
17. The retina was flat without evidence of whitening or Hollenhorst plaques.
18. Humphrey visual fields were full.
19. Normal retinal nerve fiber and ganglion cell layer thickness were observed in each eye on optical coherence tomography.
20. Computed tomography of the head revealed no change in orbital lesion size with Valsalva maneuver (Figure, B).

B: Biopsy orbital mass

5. Bibasilar coarse crackles and pretibial edema were also noted.
6. A complete blood count had results within normal limits.
7. The serum lactate dehydrogenase level was 278 U/L (to convert to microkatal per liter, multiply by 0.0167).
8. A chest radiographic image showed bibasilar infiltrates.
9. An electrocardiogram was notable for atrial fibrillation, and echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular function, mild right atrial and ventricular dilatation, and severe tricuspid regurgitation (transtricuspid pressure gradient, 40 mm Hg).

11. Para-aortic and inguinal lymphadenopathies were also noted.
12. Presumptive diagnoses of pulmonary hypertension (PH) and right-sided heart failure were made.
13. The patient began receiving dobutamine and furosemide, but she continuously required 2 to 10 L of oxygen, and further invasive evaluations could not be performed.
14. An echocardiogram identified aggravating PH (transtricuspid pressure gradient, 57 mm Hg).
15. A thorough physical examination identified scaly, crusty genital skin lesions pathologically compatible with extramammary Paget disease.
16. The patient deteriorated and died despite treatment.
17. An autopsy was performed (Figure, B).A, The chest computed tomography showed ground-glass opacities (white arrowheads) and consolidative lesions (a yellow arrowhead), but no evidence of thromboembolism was obtained.
18. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of the lung showed proliferation of intimal fibromuscular cells with (yellow arrowheads) or without (black arrowheads) the presence of Paget cells.
19. Yellow arrowheads show embolized Paget cells.
20. The encircled area (black arrowheads) indicates the vascular lumen, the inside of which is filled with proliferated fibromuscular cells but not Paget cells (original magnification ×400).

11. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed mild peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thinning inferiorly in both eyes.  
12. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain disclosed dysgenesis of the left cerebellar hemisphere and vermis (Figure, B).  
13. Family history and examination of other family members disclosed no similar abnormalities.

11. A computed tomography venogram demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.5 cm mass of likely vascular origin that was extending into the right common iliac vein (Figure).

### Step 1: Read excerpt
1. A man in his late 60s with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes for more than 10 years that was complicated by neuropathy and retinopathy presented with persistent chorea in the left upper extremity for about 1 month despite aggressive correction with insulin.
2. He was alert and oriented with healthy vital signs.
3. No evidence of cognitive impairments was present on bedside testing results.
4. The patient denied any recent infections and risk for human immunodefiency virus (HIV) infection.
5. Neurological examination results were significant for choreiform and hemiballistic movements involving the left upper extremity.
6. His home medications were carefully reviewed to rule out any medications that could cause chorea.
7. A review of his previous records indicated an admission to an outside facility 3 weeks beforehand with severe hyperglycemia and a hemoglobin A1c level of 14.1% (to convert to the proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01).
8. Despite an aggressive correction of blood glucose levels and metabolic correction, his choreiform movements had remained unresolved.
9. On admission, a complete electrolyte and toxicology panel, including calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, yielded normal results.
10. The patient’s serum glucose level was 159 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555) and his hemoglobin A1c was 10.9% without ketoacidosis.
11. Test results for antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulants, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.
12. Serum thyrotropin levels, liver function test results, and parathyroid hormone levels were healthy.
13. Copper studies, a peripheral smear, and a routine electroencephalogram yielded normal results.
14. A general screening for cancers yielded negative results.
15. The patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure), which showed a T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion.
16. Oral administration of olanzapine, 2.5 mg daily, in divided doses with careful monitoring of blood glucose levels resulted in the complete resolution of chorea.
17. Magnetic resonance imaging shows T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head (A) and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion (B).

### Step 1: Read excerpt

1. A 58-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of severe and progressive action tremor in his dominant hand when writing.  
2. When questioned, he described subtle balance problems without falls developing over the past 3 years.  
3. With the exception of profound difficulties with handwriting, motor symptoms did not affect livelihood or activities of daily living.  
4. There was no tremor reported in the nondominant hand or other limbs or symptoms of autonomic dysfunction.  
5. Neither he nor his wife reported any changes in cognitive function.  
6. His medical history comprised surgeries of the hand (laceration repair), leg (fracture repair), knee (reconstruction), and ear (stapedectomy); these were not related to the presenting symptoms.  
7. He had a family history of ischemic heart disease (both parents) but no family history of neurological disorder.  
8. He exercised regularly (5 times per week) and consumed 2 to 4 standard drinks per week.  
9. He was a former smoker with a 2-year pack history and denied any illicit drug use.  
10. Cognitive testing revealed deficits in executive function and speed of information processing.  
11. Examination of eye movements and speech revealed jerky eye pursuit, saccadic dysmetria, and moderate slurring of speech.  
12. Additional motor signs included abnormal handwriting (Figure 1A), bilateral intention tremor, mild rigidity (upper extremities), and moderately impaired heel tapping.  
13. Facial expression was normal.  
14. There was no head or resting tremor.  
15. He demonstrated moderate body sway while standing, was unable to stand on 1 foot for more than 10 seconds, and had impaired tandem walking.  
16. Gait, posture, and walking capacities during a timed 6-m walk were normal.  
17. A, Handwriting task from the motor examination showing abnormal handwriting.  
18. B, T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery image from brain magnetic resonance imaging showing white matter hyperintensities in the middle cerebellar peduncles.  
19. Routine blood test results were normal.  
20. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed moderate volume loss in the cerebral hemispheres bilaterally as well as the cerebellum and brainstem.  
21. Abnormal signal intensity was noted in the cerebral hemispheric white matter bilaterally, the middle cerebellar peduncles (Figure 1B), the cerebellar white matter, and the pons.

B: Vascular dementia

3. Physical examination showed annular erythematous plaques of up to 2 cm in diameter, with violaceous and crusted centers on the neck and trunk.

6. Blood culture results were negative.
7. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor analogs had not been prescribed to the patient.
8. Skin biopsy from a lesion on the left chest was performed for histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses (Figure, B-D).

12. D, An immunohistochemical image showing myeloperoxidase-positive cells.

16. The topical prednisolone was stopped.
17. Findings on presentation and follow-up.

1. A 72-year-old man presented with mild proximal weakness developing into progressive camptocormia, head drop, and prominent dysphagia over a 2-year period.
2. He reported a 20-kg weight loss and numbness to the ankles.
3. His medical history was significant for thyroid cancer treated with total thyroidectomy resulting in a chronic left accessory nerve injury, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and gout.
4. His medications were metformin, allopurinol, perindopril, thyroxine, and rabeprazole.
5. He had no history of smoking and drank 3 glasses of wine per week.
6. His family history was unremarkable.
7. Examination revealed significant wasting of proximal and paraspinal muscles with a flexed spine posture in the upright position (Figure 1A).
8. He had symmetric Medical Research Council grade 4/5 weakness of neck flexion, shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and extension, and hip flexion and extension bilaterally.
9. He had weakness of left shoulder elevation and winging of the left scapula secondary to the accessory nerve injury.
10. His deep tendon reflexes were normal and symmetric.
11. Pinprick sensation was reduced in both feet.
12. Lateral profile of the patient (A) revealing a flexed spine posture (camptocormia) with marked generalized muscle atrophy.
13. B, A Gömöri trichrome stain of frozen left vastus muscle (original magnification ×400) reveals 3 atrophic muscle fibers with a patchy granular appearance (red arrowheads).
14. Metabolic, endocrine, autoimmune, and infectious screens had unremarkable findings.
15. Creatine kinase levels were normal.
16. A myositis panel demonstrated low-positive Mi2 antibodies.
17. Serum electrophoresis and immunofixation identified a small immunoglobulin G (IgG) κ paraprotein with normal findings on bone marrow biopsy.
18. A whole-body positron emission tomography scan was normal.
19. Nerve conduction studies revealed a mild axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy.
20. Concentric needle electromyography showed no spontaneous activity with widespread small, brief, polyphasic units, particularly in proximal and axial muscles, consistent with a myopathic process.
21. An initial deltoid muscle biopsy did not show evidence of myopathy.
22. Because the patient’s symptoms were worsening, a second muscle biopsy of vastus lateralis was performed.

10. The posterior segment was unremarkable, with no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or macular edema.  
11. Routine investigations returned results of an elevated alkaline phosphatase level (230 U/L) and mild-positive (1:160) antinuclear antibody speckled pattern.  
12. The complete blood cell count and coagulation profile were normal.  
13. The results for extractable nuclear antigen antibodies, antidouble-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid, rheumatoid factor, human leukocyte antigen B27, QuantiFERON-TB Gold (Quest Diagnostics), syphilis serology, elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level, and a chest radiography were all negative.  
14. Topical dexamethasone, 0.1%, and homatropine, 2%, were commenced, with complete resolution of uveitic signs within 2 weeks.  
15. Dexamethasone frequency was initially once hourly for 3 days and was followed by a standard weekly tapering course.

2. The patient noted 4 years of progressive, decreased, patchy pigmentation of both eyes; constant photophobia; and constant decreased visual acuity.

4. He denied other prior ocular history, trauma, or eye surgery.
5. A review of systems had no remarkable findings, and the patient denied a prodromal viral illness.
6. On presentation, his best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20-2 OD and 20/25 OS, with a refraction of −6.25 OD and −5.50 OS (spherical equivalent).
7. The intraocular pressure was 18 OU.
8. Gonioscopy showed openness to the ciliary body with 1+ trabecular meshwork pigmentation, without synechiae or angle recession in either eye.
9. A slitlamp examination demonstrated quiet conjunctiva, clear corneas, deep and quiet anterior chambers, mid-dilated round pupils, patchy iris atrophy, and transillumination defects bilaterally (Figure).
10. Ophthalmoscopy showed an 0.8 cup-disc ratio without notching bilaterally but had otherwise normal results.
11. Retinal nerve fiber layer optical coherence tomography showed borderline thinning with normal Humphrey visual fields in both eyes.
12. Anterior segment photographs of the right eye (A) and left eye (B) showing clear corneas, patchy iris atrophy of both irides (arrowheads), and round mid-dilated pupils without posterior synechiae.

1. A 59-year-old woman with a 5-year history of intermittent bilateral uveitis and scleritis presented with painful left uveitis and an episcleral nodule (Figure 1).

3. Visual acuity was 20/30 in the left eye and 20/25 in the right eye.
4. She had been taking 60 mg of oral prednisone; topical prednisolone acetate, 1%; and oral ibuprofen for 10 days without relief.
5. She was suspected of being a steroid responder due to elevated intraocular pressure bilaterally.
6. Three years prior, sinus pressure symptoms led to magnetic resonance imaging that revealed a nasal sinus mass.
7. Biopsy demonstrated a histiocytic infiltrate with emperipolesis, consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease.
8. Timolol-dorzolamide topical drops were initiated.
9. Staging evaluations showed no other sites of RDD disease.Pretreatment.

6. 7. She developed diarrhea 1 day after admission.

11. Antigen and toxin test results for Clostridium difficile in the stool were positive.
12. Total body skin examination was notable for 1- and 3-cm tender, round perianal ulcers with a clean base.
13. Another 4-mm round ulcer was present at the superior intergluteal cleft (Figure, A).
14. There were no ocular or oral ulcers.
15. A biopsy specimen of a perianal ulcer border was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B-D).
16. Clinical and histologic images of multiple perianal ulcers.

18. A smaller, third ulcer was also noted in the intergluteal cleft.
19. B, Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy on low magnification reveals epidermal ulceration and mixed dermal inflammation (hemoxylin-eosin.
20. C, On higher magnification, the epidermis lacks viral cytopathic changes but there are enlarged dermal fibroblasts and endothelial cells (hemoxylin-eosin).
21. D, Higher magnification reveals large fibroblasts and endothelial cells with glassy cytoplasm and intranuclear inclusions (hemoxylin-eosin).

7. The mass also extended posteriorly and deformed the anterior aspect of the pons (not shown).  
8. After symptom onset, the mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (not shown).  
9. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis.  
10. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing.  
11. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally.  
12. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark.  
13. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation.  
14. No exophthalmos was noted.  
15. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.  
16. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing.  
17. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia.

2. He reported episodic breathlessness, cough, and wheezing with expectoration of brownish sputum, exacerbated with exposure to hay dust, in the past 5 years.
3. He also reported recent-onset headache while reading.
4. Physical examination revealed a depressed plaque measuring 6 × 4 cm in the right infraorbital region, surrounded by multiple nodules of sizes ranging from 1 × 1 cm to 5 × 1 cm (Figure, A).
5. The nodules were firm, mobile, and nontender on palpation.
6. Local temperature was normal.
7. There was proptosis of the right eye with mild restriction of extraocular movements on lateral gaze.
8. Examination of the oral cavity revealed dental caries, while gingivolabial sulcus was free on bidigital examination.
9. Nasal mucosa was normal.
10. Respiratory system examination revealed occasional polyphonic wheeze.
11. Chest radiography imaging showed nodular opacities in right upper zone and bronchiectasis.
12. Punch biopsy from 1 nodule was sent for histopathological and microbiological examination (Figure, B and C).
13. A, Destructive depressed plaque involving the medial half of the right side of the face surrounded by multiple nodules of varying sizes.
14. B, Hematoxylin-eosin stain of skin biopsy specimen showing inflammatory infiltrate composed of giant cells in the deeper dermis extending into the subcutaneous fat.
15. C, High-power view showing epithelioid cell granulomas and fungal profiles within giant cells (arrowheads).
16. D, Periodic acid–Schiff stain highlighting septate fungal hyphae with acute-angled branching within giant cells.

13. Waxy nodular lesions are present along the upper and lower eyelids of the patient’s left eye.
14. The younger brother had similar, although less severe, ocular and systemic findings, including eyelid nodules, facial scarring, hyperkeratosis, oral mucosal lesions, and dysphonia.
15. The patients’ parents denied consanguinity.

7. An optical coherence tomographic image of the left eye showed a large neurosensory detachment with overlying and surrounding cystoid macular edema.  
8. Fluorescein angiography of the left eye demonstrated hypofluorescence without pooling or leakage of fluorescein dye over the area of neurosensory detachment, which was persistent in later frames (Figure 1B).  
9. A, Fundus photograph of left eye showing neurosensory detachment.  
10. B, Photograph of left eye with fluorescein angiography showing hypofluorescence over area of neurosensory detachment and macular edema without associated capillary leakage or dye pooling.

13. Findings on cardiovascular, pulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.
14. Left, Dorsum of the hands, exhibiting symmetric scaly eruption.
15. Right, Bilateral lower extremities showing ruptured bullae on an erythematous brawny peeling base.
16. Laboratory studies showed mild hyponatremia (132 mmol/L) and an otherwise normal basic metabolic panel.
17. Other laboratory values were as follows: C-reactive protein, 0.58 mg/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 23 mm/h; total protein, 4.8 g/dL; and albumin, 1.8 g/dL.

19. Results of liver function tests, coagulation tests, urinalysis, thyroid function tests, measurement of serum vitamin B12 and folic acid levels, and cosyntropin stimulation tests were normal.
20. Serum copper level was 46 μg (reference range, 66-130 μg) and zinc level was 23 μg (reference, ≥80 μg).
21. Abdominal computed tomography revealed no abnormalities.

8. Two weeks after initial presentation, the visual acuity in the right eye progressed to no light perception.  
9. Repeated MRI showed progression of the lesion with masslike expansion at the chiasm measuring 1.3 cm (anterior-posterior) × 1.5 cm (craniocaudal) × 1.1 cm (transverse).  
10. The left visual field remained full.  
11. Transorbital biopsy of the right optic nerve for grading and immunohistochemistry Transcranial resection of the orbital, canalicular, and prechiasmal optic nerve Chemotherapy and/or radiation for presumptive optic nerve glioma Observation given progression to no light perception vision

3. Imaging results showed mild disease progression (new ascites and periportal metabolic lymph node).

6. The initial workup included ultrasonography and urinalysis.
7. Ultrasonography results showed abnormal intraparenchymal flow to both kidneys without evidence of kidney artery stenosis.
8. Urine studies were consistent with prerenal etiology, while the presence of casts suggested acute tubular necrosis.
9. Nephrotoxic medications (omeprazole/pantoprazole) were discontinued.
10. The top differential diagnoses at this juncture included contrast-induced nephropathy or immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)–induced acute interstitial nephritis, and empirical high dose steroids were prescribed.
11. Despite observation and steroid treatment, his sCr levels continued to increase over the next 5 days, peaking at 5.8 mg/dL, and the patient progressed into anuric kidney failure, requiring hemodialysis.
12. This prompted a kidney biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Figure).
13. One week later, he received encorafenib, a BRAF inhibitor.
14. Two weeks later, the patient’s kidney function began to improve, and hemodialysis was discontinued.
15. He continued to show gradual improvement, with a return to near baseline kidney function (sCr level, 1.3 mg/dL) approximately 6 weeks after treatment initiation.
16. Histopathology (original magnification x40) of kidney capillaries with hematoxylin and eosin stain showing atypical cells (arrowheads) (A), tubules with hematoxylin and eosin stain (B), and capillaries with melanin-A (C).

14. 1. A man aged 48 years was followed up for bilateral proliferative diabetic retinopathy, having previously been treated with panretinal photocoagulation as well as macular laser for diabetic macular edema (DME) in each eye several years ago.

8. The patient was observed for 2 weeks with the hope the implant would settle down or move out of the visual axis, but this did not happen.
9. Optos image of the patient’s right eye.
10. The fluocinolone acetonide intravitreal implant can be seen in the middle of the vitreous cavity, very close to the visual axis.
11. Additionally, panretinal photocoagulation laser scars and a superior area of fibrosis can be seen.

10. B, Dense neutrophilic infiltrate.
11. Note associated tissue necrosis.
12. Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20.
13. C, Organisms seen on Gram stain.
14. Original magnification ×60.

### Step 1: Read excerpt

1. A man in his 30s presented with a 3-month history of fourth finger right hand articular heat, pain, redness, and swelling.
2. Similar symptoms subsequently spread to the left hallux and ankle, and he developed a fever.
3. Despite many medical consultations and various attempts at treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories, the patient developed widespread arthritis within the following month, which was predominant in the knee, shoulder, and hip.
4. In the month before presentation the articular symptoms worsened, the joints had become tender, and ill-defined skin nodules had appeared predominantly on the legs (Figure, A and B).
5. An acute abdominal pain in the left hypochondrium developed, accompanied by nausea and vomiting, which led to a diagnosis of pancreatitis.
6. The patient was admitted to the hospital and clinical measures relieved the pain.
7. Laboratory test results revealed strikingly high levels of lipase and amylase, as well as normal levels of cancer antigen 19-9.
8. Bone computed tomography (CT) of the right shoulder and knee demonstrated cortical bone destruction and intraosseous medullary necrosis (Figure, C and D).
9. An abdominal CT was performed (Figure, E), and the patient underwent surgery.
10. Cancer-associated pancreatitis, panniculitis, and polyarthritis syndrome (PPP) syndrome

1. A woman in her 50s presented for evaluation of a growing, painful scar on the right side of her abdomen.  
2. She reported having a rectangular area of discolored skin for the past 10 years that developed as a result of a complication during an interventional radiology procedure for treatment of a splenic aneurysm.  
3. Two months prior to presentation this lesion became painful and enlarged, without improvement with triamcinolone cream or oral antibiotics.  
4. She also reported recent fevers, night sweats, nausea, and fatigue.  
5. She denied international travel, drug use, incarceration, and high-risk sexual behavior.  
6. The patient had a history of uterine cancer at age 25, for which she underwent hysterectomy and chemotherapy.  
7. She also had a history of breast cancer in her 40s, for which she underwent lumpectomy and tamoxifen therapy.  
8. She had undergone surgical excision of a gastric polyp in her early 50s.  
9. She had no history of radiation therapy.  
10. On physical examination she was well-appearing and afebrile, with normal vital signs.  
11. There was a 12 × 7–cm indurated pink and deep purple plaque on the right side of the abdomen, with 2 focal areas of ulceration (Figure).  
12. Extending outward from this plaque were finger-like projections of purple subcutaneous papules.  
13. Inferior to the plaque there was an approximately 3-cm, tender, orange-to-yellow patch.  
14. No lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were noted.
